anchor: The time you won your town
title: Title and context
short: Poem XIX of A Shropshire Lad (1896): an elegy addressed to a young champion runner, praising him for dying before his fame faded.
body: A Shropshire Lad, Housman's sequence of sixty-three lyrics, was privately financed and published in 1896. Many of the poems concern young men dying early. This one is an apostrophe: the speaker, one of the townsmen, addresses the dead athlete. Its argument, that early death preserves glory, has classical roots in the Greek idea that those loved by the gods die young, and in the tradition of the athletic victory ode; but the tone is ambiguous, praising the athlete in a way that is also bleak. Some biographers relate Housman's preoccupation with young men to his love for his friend Moses Jackson, though this poem is not about any known person.

anchor: Man and boy stood cheering by
title: Metre and couplets
short: Seven quatrains of rhyming couplets in tetrameter, mixing iambic and headless (trochaic-sounding) lines.
body: Each stanza rhymes aabb in four-stress lines; many begin with a stressed syllable (headless iambic or trochaic tetrameter), giving the brisk, song-like movement typical of A Shropshire Lad. The epigrammatic couplets suit the poem's paradoxes ('early though the laurel grows / It withers quicker than the rose'). Critics note the contrast between the jaunty, almost ballad-like music and the grave subject, which creates much of the poem's irony.

anchor: We chaired you through the market-place
title: chaired
short: To 'chair' a victor is to carry him aloft in triumph, on a chair or on the shoulders.
body: The OED gives 'chair' (verb) as to carry someone in a chair or on shoulders in triumph, a custom for winners of elections and contests. The image of being borne 'shoulder-high' through the market-place of a country town is repeated in stanza 2 for the funeral, where the dead runner is carried in his coffin. The parallel between triumph and funeral procession is the poem's central structural irony.

title: shoulder-high … home
short: The victory procession of stanza 1 is repeated, with the phrase order reversed, as the funeral procession.
body: Stanza 2 echoes stanza 1 with chiasmus: 'home we brought you shoulder-high' becomes 'Shoulder-high we bring you home'. 'Home' now means the grave, and 'threshold' the entrance to the tomb. 'The road all runners come' is death, the course that every runner eventually completes; the race imagery turns into the common journey to the grave. The shift from past ('brought') to present ('bring') marks the change from memory to the funeral now taking place.

sources.cite: A. E. Housman, A Shropshire Lad (1896), no. XIX, Project Gutenberg text

title: a stiller town
short: The graveyard is pictured as a quieter town, of which the athlete is now a citizen.
body: The metaphor of the grave as a town or city of the dead is ancient: the Greek 'necropolis' means city of the dead. Housman's comparative 'stiller' implies the living town is already relatively still, so the line combines rural understatement with finality. The dead become 'townsmen' of a new community, an idea developed in stanza 7, where they 'flock to gaze' at the newcomer.

anchor: Smart lad, to slip betimes away
title: Smart lad … betimes
short: 'Smart' here means clever or shrewd; 'betimes' means early, in good time.
body: 'Betimes' (archaic) means early or in good season. The colloquial 'Smart lad' praises the athlete for a shrewd move, as if dying young were a tactical decision in a race. The phrase is shockingly matter-of-fact, which is the source of much of the poem's dark irony. Readers debate whether this praise is sincere consolation or an ironic exposure of the speaker's bleak view; Housman's poems characteristically leave both possibilities open.

title: laurel … rose
short: The laurel crown of victory withers even faster than the rose, the traditional emblem of brief beauty.
body: In ancient Greece victors at the Pythian Games at Delphi were crowned with laurel, sacred to Apollo since the myth of Daphne, transformed into a laurel tree (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). The rose, by contrast, is the classic emblem of transient beauty and youth. The paradox inverts expectation: the evergreen laurel, image of enduring fame, fades faster than the short-lived rose. Glory 'does not stay' in the fields of competition, so the young athlete who dies at the moment of victory escapes the slow eclipse that awaits champions who live on.

title: the record cut
short: His record will be broken ('cut') by a later runner, but the dead cannot see it.
body: To 'cut' a record means to lower or better the existing best time, thereby breaking it. Sporting records and times were becoming a matter of public interest in the 1890s with the growth of organised athletics. The dead athlete's eyes, shut by 'the shady night', will not witness his own achievement being superseded. The following couplet ('silence sounds no worse than cheers / After earth has stopped the ears') takes the same consolation from hearing: death makes failure and acclaim equal.

title: rout
short: 'Rout' here is an archaic word for a crowd or throng.
body: 'Rout' (from Old French route, a company or band) meant a disorderly crowd or company, a sense now archaic and separate from 'rout' meaning defeat. To 'swell the rout' is to add to the crowd of former champions who 'wore their honours out', who lived to see their fame fade. The word possibly also carries the military sense of a disorderly retreat, which fits the image of champions falling back from glory.

title: Runners whom renown outran
short: A witty reversal: fame, which the runners once raced to win, now runs faster than they do and leaves them behind.
body: The race metaphor applies to fame itself: the athletes who once outran rivals are now outrun by their renown, which passes on to others. The following line, 'And the name died before the man', states the plain meaning: their fame dies before they do. The neat inversion is typical of Housman's epigrammatic technique and his debt to Latin and Greek elegy.

title: the sill of shade
short: The threshold of the underworld, the realm of 'shades' or ghosts of the dead.
body: A 'sill' is the threshold or lower beam of a doorway, and the 'lintel' is the upper beam. 'Shade' carries its classical sense of a ghost or the underworld (Latin umbra, the shades of the dead). The athlete sets his 'fleet foot', the swift foot of the runner, on the threshold of the land of the dead. In the following couplet he holds up the trophy 'to the low lintel' of a low doorway, which suggests the grave or tomb, so the door is both the house of Hades and the cramped entrance of the grave.

title: challenge-cup
short: A trophy held by a champion until another wins it from him; by dying undefeated, he keeps it forever.
body: A challenge cup is a trophy that remains with the winner only until he is defeated in a later contest. 'Still-defended' means not yet lost, and also, with a pun on 'still', 'defended forever in stillness'. The athlete's death makes his tenure permanent: he will never be challenged again. The image combines the modern sporting world of trophies with the classical image of the dead bringing their attributes into Hades.

title: early-laurelled head
short: The head crowned early with victory's laurel; the compound echoes the laurel of stanza 3.
body: The compound adjective recalls 'early though the laurel grows' and makes the crown a sign both of precocious triumph and early death. The image of the shades crowding to look at the newcomer resembles scenes in Homer's and Virgil's underworlds, where the ghosts gather around a living or newly arrived visitor (Odyssey 11; Aeneid 6). The athlete becomes an object of wonder among the dead, as he was among the living townsfolk.

title: the strengthless dead
short: Recalls Homer's formula for the dead in the underworld, 'the strengthless heads of the dead'.
body: Homer repeatedly calls the dead in Hades 'nekuon amenena karena', usually translated 'the strengthless (or powerless) heads of the dead' (Odyssey 10.521, 536; 11.29, 49). Housman, a professional classical scholar, uses the epithet to place his Shropshire athlete in the Homeric underworld. The contrast is pointed: the dead lack strength, while the athlete was strong; yet he is now one of them. The shades 'flock to gaze', like the ghosts that crowd around Odysseus.

anchor: The garland briefer than a girl
title: The garland briefer than a girl's
short: The victor's garland, though preserved 'unwithered' by death, was still briefer than a girl's: a crux about what kind of garland is meant.
body: The last line is a paradox. The laurel is 'unwithered', preserved by the athlete's death, yet it is 'briefer than a girl's' garland. One reading: the laurel, a wreath that lasts only briefly, is compared with a girl's garland of flowers, proverbially short-lived; death has kept it 'unwithered' while its natural life is briefer still. Another reading takes 'a girl's' to refer to a girl's bloom or beauty, suggesting that the athlete's glory, like his life, was as brief as youthful beauty proverbially is. A third emphasises the feminine comparison, which slightly diminishes the heroic athlete. The closure is deliberately ambiguous and ironic rather than consoling.
